title: Falcons to sign Bijan Robinson to 3-year extension that resets RB market: Sources The signing comes after a short contract standoff. The 24-year-old Texas product led the NFL with 2,298 all-purpose yards last year. Josh Kendall and Jonathan Jones 83
summary:
Robinson is the third of Atlanta’s young stars to agree to a long-term deal this offseason, joining Drake London and Kyle Pitts. Kevin C. Cox / Getty Images
There will be no more holding in for Bijan Robinson in Atlanta. The Falcons and their star running back agreed Tuesday to a three-year extension worth up to $75 million that resets the market for the position, according to league sources with knowledge of the contract who spoke anonymously because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
full_text:
Robinson is the third of Atlanta’s young stars to agree to a long-term deal this offseason, joining Drake London and Kyle Pitts. Kevin C. Cox / Getty Images
There will be no more holding in for Bijan Robinson in Atlanta. The Falcons and their star running back agreed Tuesday to a three-year extension worth up to $75 million that resets the market for the position, according to league sources with knowledge of the contract who spoke anonymously because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The deal makes Robinson the highest-paid running back in NFL history with the base value worth $22.25 million per year, and the extension includes $51 million in guaranteed money.
The two sides have been in negotiations for months. And while the Falcons committed more than $290 million to three core players this summer, the deal with Robinson took more time and resulted in Robinson not practicing for the majority of the first week of training camp.
Robinson is the third of Atlanta’s young stars to agree to a long-term deal this offseason, joining wide receiver Drake London , who signed a four-year, $141 million extension on June 8, and tight end Kyle Pitts , who agreed to a three-year, $56 million extension on June 23. The team also secured a long-term deal with guard Matthew Bergeron, who signed a four-year extension with $60 million guaranteed on Aug. 1.
“I’m really excited to help lead this team and the offense to great heights,” Robinson said during the Falcons’ minicamp in mid-June.
The 24-year-old product of the University of Texas led the NFL with 2,298 all-purpose yards last year, and no player has more than his 5,648 yards from scrimmage in the last three years. Only Saquon Barkley and Derrick Henry have more than Robinson’s 3,910 rushing yards in that span.
“I’ve been around some good running backs, but obviously you know how I feel about Bijan,” Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski, who coached Adrian Peterson in Minnesota and Nick Chubb in Cleveland, said. “I would start with just the pro he is. I appreciate how he goes about his business in the meeting room, how he goes about his business on the grass. The physical skill set is obvious off of the tape. Certainly, on the grass, he’s somebody that can affect the game in a multitude of ways, but I would pivot back to just the person that he is and the impact that he has on our roster, our locker room, on a daily basis.”
Robinson was the eighth pick in the 2023 NFL Draft, becoming the highest-drafted running back since Barkley was taken second overall by the Giants in 2018. He immediately made enough of a splash in Atlanta that his success paved the way for the Las Vegas Raiders to pick Ashton Jeanty sixth in 2025 and the Cardinals to take Jeremiyah Love third this spring.
The Falcons exercised the fifth-year option on Robinson’s contract earlier this year, which would have kept him with the team at least through the 2027 season, but even then, first-year general manager Ian Cunningham was hopeful of getting a long-term deal done this summer.
This fall, Robinson is hoping to top last year’s career-best numbers, but he’s also hoping to make his first playoff appearance as a pro.
“Individual goals are great, but I’m going to continue to be the guy the team can rely on,” he said. “Like I say every year, I’m just trying to be better than I was last year in all aspects of my game. … Last year was a cool year, but this year I want to be even better.”
Stefanski’s staff will be the third Robinson has played for in his short career.
“You just have to be really adaptable,” Robinson said. “I have learned a lot of different personalities. I’ve seen a lot of different things in this building. I think a lot of them have been great people, great coaches.”
No player has more than Robinson’s 1,003 offensive touches since he joined the league in 2023, and the new coaching staff has already made clear it doesn’t plan on cutting his workload any.
“Bijan loves football,” offensive coordinator Tommy Rees said. “That’s where it starts. What a special human being. He’s eager to do a lot.”
Bijan will be joined in the backfield this year by free-agent addition Brian Robinson.
“He’s a great guy,” Brian Robinson said of Bijan. “He is exactly what you see. He comes to work every day prepared to be his best. It’s no surprise that he plays the way he plays.”
Bijan Robinson’s new deal comes amid his growing international fame, which was highlighted during this summer’s World Cup by his friendships with France’s Kylian Mbappe and Brazil’s Vinicius Jr.
“They are bigger than most celebrities, really all celebrities in America,” Robinson said. “It’s really cool to see how they handle it.”
Robinson and Vinicius have bonded in part through their relationship with celebrity jeweler Leo Khusro, also known as Leo Frost.
“We always text each other after games,” Robinson said. “He watches all our games. He would send me the highlights from the game. It’s cool to hang out with him. He’s such a great dude. He’s a really, really good person. What he does on the field and what I do on the field, there are a lot of similarities. I’m excited to see what he can do in the World Cup.”
Robinson traveled to Italy and France earlier this year to do promotional work for the NFL and himself, and he’ll be in Spain in November for the Falcons game against the Bengals in Madrid, where he plans to reunite with Mbappe, who plays professionally for Real Madrid, as well as two other friends from the Spanish team.
“The life that (the soccer players) live out there and how they go about their business is pretty inspiring,” he said. “They are very organized and team-oriented.”

full_text:
Jack Strand, an undrafted rookie quarterback from Minnesota State Moorhead, was thrust into a surprising role at the start of Falcons training camp. Todd Kirkland / Getty Images
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — Kendal Daniels thought his job was stressful. Then he saw Jack Strand’s homework.
“I sit next to him in some of the rookie meetings, and I see his playbook, and I’m like, ‘ Man … ’” Daniels, the Atlanta Falcons’ rookie linebacker, said. “I feel the stress going out there with the first group, but as the quarterback … I couldn’t imagine being in his spot right now. I really couldn’t.”
Strand couldn’t imagine it 10 days ago. The 22-year-old quarterback from Bloomer, Wis., was an undrafted afterthought out of Division II Minnesota State Moorhead way back then.
Then Michael Penix Jr.’s surgeon delayed the quarterback’s full return to practice.
Then Tua Tagovailoa’s back tightened up.
Then the Falcons released third-string quarterback Trevor Siemian due to an injury.
And, all of a sudden, Strand was Atlanta’s starting quarterback on the first day of training camp. He learned that news the night before.
“He’s handling it a lot better than I would,” Daniels said. “He’s doing great.”
Strand, in fact, handled almost all of the first-team reps in team work through the first week of training camp as Tagovailoa and Penix rehabbed and newcomer Cooper Rush learned the offense.
“It’s really impressive,” tight end Kyle Pitts said. “To be thrown in the fire like that, it’s pretty cool to see how he’s embracing it. He’s getting better. I have to give him his credit. Each day he’s coming more into it.”
Strand remains a long shot to play in the regular season, but given the health histories of the Falcons’ top two quarterbacks and the early reviews he’s getting from coaches and teammates, it’s not out of the question.
“One of the things I have been telling myself a ton,” Strand said, “is just, ‘Be where your feet are. Just enjoy the moment. Don’t dwell on any success or any mistakes you might have had. Don’t look to the future or worry about what’s going to be happening in a couple weeks.’”
Plenty is going on to occupy Strand’s mind in the present. He’s still cramming every day on the Falcons offense, a routine that includes having his girlfriend of the last seven years read the play calls to him over the phone at night so he can better recite them in the huddle.
That part is working, Pitts said.
“You can hear the deepness in his voice for sure,” the tight end said of the 6-foot-4, 240-pound quarterback. “He’s got some bass in there.”
Strand impressed the Falcons during the NFL Draft process because of his height, arm strength and intelligence, coach Kevin Stefanski said, and those traits carried over into training camp. Strand had a 3.87 GPA in engineering physics in college and was a finalist for the William V. Campbell Trophy, the premier academic award in college football.
“Jack continues to impress with his ability to command the offense, to get in and out of the huddle, get us in and out of run plays and pass plays,” Stefanski said. “He’s a very, very bright young man, and when you see him up close, he’s a big kid who can stand in the pocket and deliver.”
Strand stands noticeably higher than the rest of the quarterbacks during drills.
“That dude’s a tank, bro,” wide receiver Drake London said. “He’s a big person.”
The Falcons’ skill players are rallying around the young quarterback, London said.
“I think it’s really, really good for him, and we have the kind of people where we’re going to bear with him and keep on trying to grow with him,” London said.
Even Tagovailoa and Penix have welcomed Strand despite the threat he might pose, Strand said.
“Those guys are awesome, and they have been so welcoming to me,” Strand said. “Any questions I have, I know I can go to them, and they will help me out. It hasn’t felt like I’m lower in the QB room or whatever. They are treating me like any other QB. It’s been awesome to get a chance to work with them.”
“Dude can sling the ball,” said Tagovailoa, whose workload was increasing as the Falcons opened their second week of training camp Monday.
The Athletic ’s Dane Brugler ranked Strand as the 15th-best quarterback prospect in the 2026 draft, and when Strand went undrafted, he was one of Atlanta’s first calls. He started 42 games at MSU Moorhead, throwing for 13,161 yards, 126 touchdowns and 50 interceptions in four seasons, and he turned down transfer portal options before his senior campaign.
“It was never my intent to transfer, no matter what,” he said. “I didn’t have a ton of schools (approaching me) like some of these guys might have had, but I wanted to stay (at MSUM). They were loyal to me. They were the only ones who gave me a scholarship offer. Once I had some success there, I didn’t want to just use them as a boost to get to another school. The relationships I built with my teams and my coaches — that’s not something I wanted to leave just to go chase a paycheck.”
That loyalty has made him something of a hometown hero.
“Everyone from back home has been so supportive of me, texting me to see how things are going,” he said. “That’s such a blessing for me to hear from those people and see the support I have back home.”
Some of Strand’s youngest brother’s high school teammates, excited by his recent battlefield promotion, have gotten his phone number and now text him encouraging messages. (The middle Strand brother, Zeke, is a tight end at Augustana University in Sioux Falls, S.D.)
“Our school wasn’t really getting a lot of national attention before myself … and the guys around me got there,” Strand said, “so the years we had there and me being able to come down here and elevate that platform for the school, that’s something I have been so happy to do.”
That platform will grow if Strand makes the Falcons’ 53-man roster. It will explode if he starts a regular-season game.
“As a quarterback, you prepare to be the starter,” Stefanski said. “That’s just how you do it. Everybody has to prepare themselves like they’re the starter. That’s how that room works. That’s the nature of that position.”
For now, though, Strand isn’t thinking about that. He’s trying not to even think about tomorrow.
“I’m just taking it day by day, trying to attack every day, get better every day whether I’m getting a bunch of reps or not getting any reps,” he said. “The mindset doesn’t change, whatever reps I get. I just have to treat those reps like game reps because that’s how I get better and that’s how our team gets better.”

full_text:
Zay Flowers, a Pro Bowler in 2024 and 2025, had a career-high 86 receptions and 1,211 receiving yards last season. Joe Sargent / Getty Images
Zay Flowers has already done something no drafted Baltimore Ravens wide receiver had ever done, and the organization just made sure he’ll remain with the team for the foreseeable future.
The Ravens and Flowers reached an agreement on a contract extension, Baltimore’s latest move to reward one of its core players, the team announced Tuesday. The 25-year-old is preparing for his fourth NFL season, and a decision on his fifth-year option was due May 1. Both sides, though, had prioritized a contract extension this offseason.
The extension is for four years and worth up to $140 million, with $108 million in guaranteed money, per team sources who were not permitted to speak because financial details had not yet been released. This extension makes Flowers the fourth-highest-paid receiver in the NFL behind the Seattle Seahawks’ Jaxon Smith-Njigba ($42.15 million per year), the Cincinnati Bengals’ Ja’Marr Chase ($40.25 million) and the Atlanta Falcons’ Drake London ($35.3 million).
The Ravens and WR Zay Flowers have agreed to a four-year contract extension worth $140 million, source tells @TheAthletic . The deal includes $108M guaranteed after he put together a second straight Pro Bowl season. ESPN first to report. pic.twitter.com/xi1GvgiPZq
— Jonathan Jones (@jjones9) August 4, 2026
The deal makes Flowers the second-highest paid Raven in team history, behind only quarterback Lamar Jackson.
Flowers, a first-round pick in 2023, has made the Pro Bowl twice in three seasons. When he was selected to his first Pro Bowl in 2024, he became the first homegrown Ravens wide receiver to earn that distinction.
Flowers, the Ravens’ No. 1 receiver, has 237 catches for 3,128 yards and 16 touchdowns in his first 50 regular-season games. Since entering the NFL, he ranks 10th among wide receivers in yards and 13th in catches. He’s done it despite being in an offense that leans heavily on the run game and features multiple tight ends in its passing attack.
The former Boston College standout already ranks fifth in franchise history in receiving yards and receptions after just three seasons. He’s one of only nine Ravens to post a 1,000-yard receiving season, and he’s done it twice. His 1,211 receiving yards last season are a franchise record for a Ravens wide receiver.
Ravens WR Zay Flowers, who isn’t practicing, shared a hug on the practice field about 20 minutes ago and got good reason. Team confirms that the Ravens and Flowers have reached agreement on an extension.
— Jeff Zrebiec (@jeffzrebiec) August 4, 2026
There’s been plenty of debate outside the Ravens’ facility about whether Flowers is a legitimate No. 1 receiver. At 5-foot-9, 183 pounds, Flowers has not been a huge red zone threat, and the Ravens’ deep passing game has been spotty in recent years. He’s also had some high-profile ball-security issues.
However, Flowers has been extremely productive, averaging 13.2 yards per reception. He’s been durable. having played all but one regular-season game in three years. He’s considered one of the hardest workers on the team, and he has a strong rapport and friendship with Jackson, who backed the Ravens’ drafting of Flowers in 2023.
Flowers has provided a long-awaited counterargument to the Ravens’ long-standing troubles drafting and developing wide receivers.
The extension continues general manager Eric DeCosta’s efforts to lock in as many key Ravens as possible. Over the past year-plus, the Ravens have signed extensions with a litany of key players, including running back Derrick Henry, wide receiver Rashod Bateman, tight end Mark Andrews, left tackle Ronnie Stanley, nose tackle Travis Jones and safety Kyle Hamilton.
There was a sense of urgency with Flowers because of the rising prices in the wide receiver market. Smith-Njigba recently became the NFL’s highest-paid wide receiver after agreeing to a four-year, $168.6 million contract with the Seahawks. Overall, 19 wide receivers are earning at least $25 million per year, while another five make more the $20 million annually. Flowers now joins that group.

full_text:
Buffalo Bills linebacker Michael Hoecht waves to fans as he heads to the field during training camp at St. John Fisher University. Hoecht is recovering from last season's torn Achilles tendon. Shawn Dowd / Rochester Democrat and Chronicle / USA Today via Imagn Images
PITTSFORD, N.Y. — Michael Hoecht is a Buffalo Bills folk hero already.
The defensive lineman played only 64 snaps last year. But in the fleeting time he was on the field, the man was sensational.
“For seven quarters,” Hoecht said with a smirk, “I was the best player in football.”
Although the last play ended his season, the way he reacted made Bills fans swoon. What would be the worst moment in a mere mortal’s career, Hoecht turned into a valiant scene.
So what has been more savage to Hoecht’s teammates: How he refused to leave the sideline despite his torn Achilles tendon, or how he has attacked his recovery to be back on the practice field so fast?
“That’s a tough one,” Bills safety and fellow folk hero Damar Hamlin said. “I want to say staying on the sidelines after the injury, but the way that he’s been able to bounce back and be out here like he never lost a step? It’s f—— impressive. I won’t lie.”
Hoecht will be a difference-maker if he can recapture anything close to what he showed in his quick introduction last year.
His presence on Buffalo’s defense was pyrotechnic. He missed the first six games while serving a suspension for violating the NFL’s performance-enhancing drugs policy, then blasted into our consciousness.
In a Week 8 pasting of the Carolina Panthers, he recorded a strip-sack of Andy Dalton and later shared a sack with defensive tackle Deone Walker.
A week later against the Kansas City Chiefs, Hoecht tipped a pass — officials missed it and flagged Patrick Mahomes for intentional grounding — and one play later shared a sack with edge rusher Gregory Rousseau.
Earlier in the game, Hoecht got behind Mahomes before a pass, yet still sprinted to tackle tight end Travis Kelce from behind 20 yards downfield.
On the second play of the fourth quarter, Hoecht’s right Achilles popped.
He hopped to the Bills’ sideline, trying in vain to get there without help. A few steps away, he couldn’t go anymore, took a knee and punched the Highmark Stadium turf. He begged down judge Daniel Gallagher not to blow the whistle for an injury timeout, but the game was stopped anyway.
With the help of an athletic trainer, Hoecht was guided to a bench and plopped down in anguish. The medical staff huddled around him and told him he was done for the day — and for the season.
“The doctor squeezed my calf and said ‘10 months,’” Hoecht said, referring to standard recovery time for a torn Achilles tendon. “Oh, boy.
“I asked the doctors if it would help me at all if I go back into the locker room right now and start to do something. They said ‘No, it would not do anything.’ So I still felt like I had a job to do.”
For the Bills’ defense, it was next man up.
For Hoecht, it was next fan up.
Hoecht was wired for sound that game. What happened next, while fans were focused on the Bills closing out a big victory over their rivals, was shared soon after.
“I thought they would shut the cameras off,” Hoecht said, “but at that point, all I’m thinking is, ‘We went through OTAs and training camp and did all this work, and this will be my last time at this stadium. I’m not going anywhere. I’m going to stay here, and we’re going to win this game.’”
Hoecht’s teammates were well aware of his decision. He asked to be assisted from the offense’s bench, where he was evaluated, to the defense’s bench. He wanted to be involved. A procession of players came by to hug him, to slap his shoulder pads, to say that they love him.
Hoecht never stopped cheering or coaching.
“That’s a dude right there,” Bills running back Ty Johnson said. “That’s a guy that wants to see everyone succeed. He was having a hell of a game. What a team player to stay out there and support his team.”
Nine months later, they’re marveling at his recovery.
The Bills haven’t held a full-contact practice yet, but the staff has been working Hoecht into full team drills since training camp began.
“I’d say ‘surprised,’ but that does the word a disservice,” Hoecht’s agent, David Canter, said. “It’s more, like, ‘Yeah, it’s Michael Hoecht. Of course, he’s going to be back early. Of course, he’s going to be pushing on levels no one else can push on.’ But with Michael, when he says ‘Yeah, I’m going to be cleared,’ how are you shocked? I don’t think one person who knows him is shocked.”
Canter has experienced the flip side of Achilles recovery. Canter represented edge rusher Olivier Vernon, who ruptured his left Achilles at the end of the 2021 season. In 14 games, Vernon recorded nine sacks, a safety, a forced fumble, a recovery and three pass breakups that year, but never played again.
Hoecht praised his caregivers throughout the process for helping him recover so quickly. The surgery was performed by Achilles specialist Dr. Neal ElAttrache, with rehab overseen by Bills staffers Joe Micca and AJ Blue plus private biomechanics trainer Tom Gormely.
“I told them, ‘I literally will do whatever you say to help get me to this,’” Hoecht said of training camp, “because being out here is the best way I can ramp up to make sure I’m ready to go for Week 1.
“They were only going to let me go so far, but the deal we had was that when they felt comfortable to tell me to go, then I was going to go 100 percent. It was their job to tell me the dose, and it was my job to give 100 percent effort.”
The most torturous part was the immediate aftermath. The Bills still had nine more regular-season games, and their defensive line absolutely needed D-line help down the homestretch and in the playoffs. Hoecht knew he could have influenced games when it mattered. Instead, he watched helplessly as the season ended with a thwump.
Hoecht, who turns 29 in October, explained he was able to turn that page after the Super Bowl and learned to love rehabilitation — so much so that it almost sounded like a weird, recurring Christmas.
“I hate to say it, but it wasn’t that bad,” Hoecht said. “Every two weeks you get a new thing to do. For two weeks you’re walking. Then for two weeks you’re jogging a little bit. Then for two weeks you can jump rope. Then for two weeks you can lift.
“You get to do something new. It keeps you engaged. You’ve got to ride that wave.”
Because he didn’t spend much time on the field and suffered such a devastating injury, many pundits have overlooked the possibility he can make a difference in 2026. This time of year is when we scrutinize the new blood — the free agents and the rookies — and wonder who might move the needle.
In Hoecht’s seven quarters for Buffalo last year, TruMedia charted him for 42 pass rushes, eight pressures (only 10 Bills had more all season) and five hurries (only nine had more) for a gaudy 19.0 pressure percentage.
The first step in recapturing that kind of production is returning to the field.
“The way Mike comes out here and works, the way that he’s a pro in the meeting rooms and has been rehabbing and taking care of his body,” said Rousseau, “it’s really inspirational.”

Sam Ehlinger is getting an opportunity to compete with Jarrett Stidham in camp for the Broncos' No. 2 quarterback spot. David Zalubowski / Associated Press
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — The Denver Broncos wrapped up their first week of training camp Monday. Starting quarterback Bo Nix has looked healthy and confident as he heads into a pivotal third season . That qualifies as the most important development for a team that needs Nix at his best to chase a Super Bowl in 2026, but there have been plenty of other subplots to monitor.
Here are a few other things we’ve learned:
Coach Sean Payton was asked in March at the annual NFL league meeting in Arizona if there would be a competition for the No. 2 quarterback job between Jarrett Stidham, the team’s backup the past three seasons, and Sam Ehlinger, last year’s No. 3.
“We see competition,” Payton said then. “And it wasn’t different last year. There’s nothing that is etched in stone. There just isn’t, and that’s a good thing.”
Fast forward to the first day of training camp, when Stidham ran the second unit and Ehlinger piloted the threes, and Payton was asked again whether a competition had begun.
“There’s a competition at all these spots,” he replied. “The guard position, quarterback position, tight end position. They’re competing for playing time and reps. That’s why we don’t have a depth chart or anything like that.”
Still, there had been little to suggest, beyond Payton’s words about competition throughout the roster, that the Broncos were considering a different backup for Nix. In every practice open to the media dating back to the spring, Stidham had been ahead of Ehlinger. That changed Saturday. Ehlinger ran the No. 2 offense while Stidham, whose lone appearance last season came as Nix’s replacement in the AFC Championship Game, ran the third group. Payton cautioned afterward that he “wouldn’t make anything” out of the change of order, but it was an indication that Denver is giving the 27-year-old Ehlinger a chance to compete for a promotion.
The Broncos signed Ehlinger, a 2021 sixth-round pick of the Indianapolis Colts, to a one-year deal in free agency last season. He spent all season as the team’s No. 3 quarterback, bouncing between the practice squad and the active roster. He had several opportunities to join other teams last season while on Denver’s practice squad and again this offseason, but he chose to remain with the Broncos last season and then sign another one-year deal with the team in March — even though there was no guaranteed offer of a backup role in Denver’s recruitment pitch.
“I think we just sold our program and the offense,” Payton said. ” … We could never promise anything. … I would say this: We saw immediate growth. I think you’d have to ask him, but I think he felt like, ‘I want to continue with this offense and continue where I’m going.’ I think he felt good about it to make that decision.”
Preseason games figure to be a pivotal battleground in the competition, starting with the Broncos’ preseason opener Aug. 14 at Atlanta. Ehlinger was efficient Saturday during his run with the second team. Stidham, meanwhile, had arguably the top throw of the first week of camp when he launched a 50-yard touchdown pass to Marvin Mims, catching the fourth-year wide receiver in stride at the front of the end zone. Stidham was again quarterbacking the second unit when the Broncos resumed practice Monday after a day off.
Riley Moss matched Courtland Sutton stride for stride Monday as Nix launched a deep ball to his favorite target. Sutton appeared to have position as he turned his body to shield the cornerback while leaping for the ball. Moss, though, somehow managed to invade Sutton’s space with minimal contact and then ripped the ball away for an interception. It was arguably the top defensive play of the first week of camp. It was a free play for the offense that came after the defense jumped offside, but during camp, Broncos coaches insist that players finish plays despite penalties or would-be sacks somewhere along the way.
“It was a great play,” safety Talanoa Hufanga said of Moss’ interception. “It’s one of those where it’s 50-50 (when) the ball goes up, and when your guy comes down with it, you’re always excited.”
Moss, a third-round pick in the 2023 draft, is among a handful of key Broncos players entering contract years. The list also includes Mims, nickel Ja’Quan McMillian and safety Brandon Jones, all of whom have had strong starts.
Mims has been a consistent deep target for Denver’s quarterbacks, the aforementioned deep touchdown from Stidham being just one of several big plays he has produced. McMillian broke up a pass intended for Jaylen Waddle on Monday, marking one of the few times Denver’s defense has gotten the better of the team’s new offensive weapon.
Before his interception Monday against Sutton, Moss broke up back-to-back Nix passes during a third-down drill in Saturday’s practice. Jones, meanwhile, is fully healthy after a pectoral injury caused him to miss the final three games of the 2025 regular season and both of Denver’s playoff games. He said he feels like he picked up where he left off next to Hufanga at the back end of Denver’s defense.
The Broncos signed three starters to extensions during training camp last year (defensive end Zach Allen, Sutton, edge rusher Nik Bonitto) and extended three other players during the season (defensive tackle Malcolm Roach, center Luke Wattenberg, kicker Wil Lutz). That was the continuation of a trend that has seen the Broncos sign 11 of their players to multiyear extensions since before the 2024 season.
There will be different considerations for Denver’s extension-eligible players this time around. The Broncos have to start factoring in a possible massive extension for Nix, who will be eligible to re-sign after this season. But what’s been clear through one week of camp is that the players angling for extensions have made strong early impressions.
Payton has never believed in creating a pecking order for his wide receivers.
“We don’t have a classic third (receiver),” he said last week. “We don’t have a (No.) 1A, a 2, a 3. We’re just different than that.”
Still, it’s probably safe to assume that Sutton and Waddle, if healthy, will be the team’s two leading receivers this season. Sutton is coming off back-to-back 1,000-yard receiving seasons, and Waddle has averaged that total over his five NFL seasons. So, if there is no true WR3 in Denver’s offense — frequent personnel switches can put receivers in different positions depending on the defensive look — the question then becomes who will be the most reliable producer outside of the top two?
Pat Bryant, entering his second NFL season, has looked like a potential answer to the question through one week of camp. Catches like his leaping grab along the sideline Monday, which took place on a well-placed back-shoulder throw from Nix have become commonplace for last year’s third-round pick out of Illinois. He became a more consistent third-down target for Nix as last season progressed, the quarterback trusting Bryant to make tough catches in traffic. In Year 2, Bryant is playing at an increased tempo that comes with a greater understanding of the offense.
“He’s got some of the better hands in traffic with his feet on the ground,” Payton said. “He’s really good with the run after the catch. He’s real smart and he’s someone who can move from X (position) to the slot. It will be easy creating his role.”
Bryant played 48 percent of Denver’s offensive snaps last season and missed two games with a concussion. He appears to be in line for a bigger slice of the pie in 2026.
Wattenberg left Monday’s practice early with a medical trainer and didn’t return after what appeared to be a left arm injury. Payton said afterward that he expected the center to be fine.

full_text:
Byron Young sacks C.J. Stroud during a 2025 season in which he notched 12 sacks and earned his first Pro Bowl nod. Ronald Martinez / Getty Images
LOS ANGELES — Don’t look now, but Byron Young is allowing himself to dream again.
Just seven years ago, the Los Angeles Rams outside linebacker was behind a cash register at Dollar General . Now, he’s entering his fourth year in the NFL. Just three years ago, he heard team after team tell him he was too old as a rookie to be on their radar, and now he’s a Pro Bowler fresh off a 12-sack season.
Ask Young about where he is after 27.5 sacks in three seasons, and he describes his standing in basic terms: Reliable. Dependable.
But to really know Young, you have to ask where he’s going. That’s the Dollar General employee turned tryout football player turned military student turned statistical anomaly in him.
“I need to get to All-Pro,” Young said. “I need to be a guy where when it comes to that third down and long and we need to have it, I come through. I’ll force a bad play or force a bad decision. That’s what it is for me. I want to be that guy where they look to find, ‘OK, we need a stop. We’re behind. Or we need to seal the deal.’ I want to be one of those crunch-time situation guys.”
“Someone like Myles Garrett.”
That’s how dreams work. They can sound crazy to the outside world, but what matters is if there’s a piece of them that makes sense to the heart.
And perhaps nobody has a better view of what this outrageously high bar looks like than Young.
The Rams’ offseason blockbuster trade to send Jared Verse to the Cleveland Browns in exchange for a two-time Defensive Player of the Year and the NFL’s all-time single-season sack record holder did something to the vision sitting in Young as he enters a contract year.
He was so close with Verse, and the two built a terrific tandem, with Verse’s power collapsing the pocket to force a panicked quarterback into open grass so a speedy Young could chase him down. That duo landed two edge rushers in the Pro Bowl and had the Rams on the doorstep of the Super Bowl last season.
But like Young, Verse was a player ascending but not yet ascended. Garrett is a supercharged version, as he would be in upgrading just about any pass rusher. That’s what 125.5 sacks in nine seasons can do, and Young knows what that aura looks like after spending his rookie season on a line with Aaron Donald.
So, as Garrett begins to settle into a new home in Los Angeles, he has Young in his ear and in his shadow nearly everywhere in these various team settings.
“I just ask the questions,” Young said. “I ask for his thoughts on certain rushes and certain plays and why do you think like that?”
Garrett is an introspective character. He’ll allow his mind to zoom out a thousand feet from the spot where his 6-foot-4, 272-pound body with a chiseled six-pack is throwing a tackle onto his back and into a quarterback’s stomach. Garrett recently told Young that he has never once had a pass rush rep where he didn’t believe he could make the sack.
It sounds like simple confidence until you realize the barricade NFL teams place in front of one player to keep him from being the one to ruin their day.
“He gets chipped and he gets the slide. He gets triple-teamed and he still has the mindset of, ‘I’m going to beat that,'” Young said. “And he still beats that. He always has a plan.”
“… I’m not saying I don’t believe in every rush when I take it, but it’s understanding how powerful that is. The mind is a powerful thing. If you put a negative thought in there, you’re going to get negative results.”
And negative thoughts didn’t get Young to where he is today. They didn’t talk him down from going to that walk-on tryout practice at Georgia Military Academy between Dollar General shifts seven years ago. The devil didn’t dance on his shoulder as he stared out at hundreds of star high school players trying to crack the same handful of spots available, or when he made it there and was living in military barracks and attacking practices just in the hopes of landing a call with a cellphone that couldn’t ring because he didn’t have the money to pay the bill.
But Young’s path from then to now has been largely about making it, about proving he is somebody. Now, he’s trying to become a special somebody. Something more than reliable, worth more than a rookie contract, respected more than a Pro Bowler with a sack total. Because he knows the gaps in his game that fill the gulf between good and great.
They screamed at him in last season’s playoffs, when he banged his right knee up early on in the divisional round against the Chicago Bears, spent the night with an ice pack over it, missed a week of practice and tried to run through the fire to get his team to a Super Bowl but couldn’t. After a 12-sack breakout season, Young didn’t get to the quarterback in three playoff games. A 31-27 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in the NFC Championship Game became the symbol for the distance between dependable and reliable and something to be remembered.
So, that’s what he’s chasing now.
It’s led to a different offseason routine than in the past. Whereas he used to channel his joy to be playing football for any team into hard offseason training, he’s learning what it takes to dial back and protect that knee so that it can survive a 20-game season. After all, he’s already in his athletic prime at 28, even though he’s just entering his fourth season. And part of playing catch-up was knowing how to work smarter rather than harder.
So he spent his offseason doing yoga and Pilates. He limited his football training to a mere walk-through variety of acting out hand placements. He owns 80 different compression sleeves to drape the right knee in, to pressurize and stabilize the knee, and he sleeps in them to make the adjustment feel like muscle memory. He sometimes wears a brace. And this season, he’ll practice on a designed maintenance schedule.
His work looks inherently different now than it did when he was just trying to stand out at a walk-on tryout or create practice film in spring football to get any major college to offer a scholarship. He isn’t looking for believers anymore. That’s what he found living in his corner by joining a team led by Sean McVay, a coach who called him twice at random this offseason just to check in on life.
“You want to talk about a guy that’s mentally and physically tough?” McVay said. “He looks like the statue of David out here, but he’s awesome. I love everything about him. … He can create on his own. I think he does a great job on some of the two- and three-man games where he’s a tight wrapper, looper. He’s got position flex where he can be an underneath zone defender, but we like him when he’s going forward a lot more often than not. He’s all about the right stuff.”
The Rams don’t have to worry about whether Young will commit to the grind. They see it all season long, like when he carries an iPad everywhere just to steal moments watching extra film where they exist, including over lunch in the team cafeteria. Those are the quiet moments where the dreams start to sound less crazy.
“The dude is just a worker,” defensive lineman Kobie Turner said. “You see it in the locker room, you see it just around the building, but you also see it on the tape.”
Young has among the best chances of any Rams player to cash in this season. He’ll be playing opposite the double-teams, chips, slide protections and game plans coming Garrett’s way. He’ll rush with two-time All-Pro Trent McDuffie as well as Jaylen Watson, Quentin Lake and Kam Curl, who all just signed the types of extensions he’s chasing now.
“I love this team,” Young said. “Whatever happens happens, but this is the team I want to be with. I want to be with the L.A. Rams.”
The Garrett and McDuffie acquisitions are going to make it challenging for the Rams to retain Young, especially considering that wide receiver Puka Nacua, Turner, guards Steve Avila and Kevin Dotson and right…

full_text:
Patriots quarterback Drake Maye looks to have even more command in his second season in Josh McDaniels' offense. Eric Canha / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of NFL training camp .
The New England Patriots’ practice Monday ended with yet another touchdown pass to Kayshon Boutte. He’s been so good through the first week that any fans following the team’s training camp likely know what kind of start he’s off to.
But camp is about more than just a wide receiver playing well. So today, we’ll break down the offense with one thought on every player. The defense is up tomorrow.
QB Drake Maye: This may seem like a small thing, but Maye looks even more comfortable than last season — and he has been able to do more. More command over the offense. More familiarity in the scheme. More on his plate. That should lead to another great season.
QB Tommy DeVito: Maye didn’t miss any games a year ago, but if he has to, the Patriots like having a backup with starting experience. His arm strength doesn’t pop, but he checks the box for someone who could make a spot start.
QB Behren Morton: He’s gotten more snaps so far than a typical third-string quarterback, which speaks to the Patriots’ plan of — ideally — developing him into Maye’s backup next season.
RB Rhamondre Stevenson: I think Stevenson has done enough to keep the Patriots’ backfield workload at 50-50. He just needs to hang onto the ball and build on the 13 straight games in which he hasn’t fumbled.
RB TreVeyon Henderson: It’s looked a bit like last season: big, explosive plays, but just enough mistakes in pass protection that it feels like a risk to use him on third downs. If he can improve in that skill, though, look out.
RB Lan Larison: He lacks explosiveness out of the backfield, which is more noticeable given the speed around him in the competition for the No. 3 spot, and will need to show some running savvy in the preseason to win the gig.
RB Jam Miller: The speed is obvious, and it could make him a factor in the kick-return game. Those will be important reps for him in the preseason games.
RB Terrell Jennings: The No. 3 running back job is wide open, especially now that Jennings participated in practice Monday, his first of the summer.
RB Myles Montgomery: The undrafted rookie is another player getting a crack at the kick-return job thanks to his speed (4.44-second 40), which shows up on outside runs too.
FB Reggie Gilliam: Added as part of the team’s goal of being a more consistent rushing team, Gilliam has been everything you’d hope so far. He had a great block on a Stevenson touchdown Monday.
WR A.J. Brown: After a (relatively and understandably) slow start, Brown has connected with Maye on some big plays and looks the part of a true No. 1 receiver. He dislocated his thumb during Monday’s practice but wanted to remain in the session and continue squaring off against Christian Gonzalez, a matchup that has lived up to the billing as a highlight of camp.
WR Romeo Doubs: He does everything pretty well. Nothing exceptional, but he’s just a good, solid receiver. Should be a good No. 2 in this offense.
WR Kayshon Boutte: The star of camp so far from an offensive perspective. If he keeps this up, he’s either increasing his value on the trade market or playing his way into a meaningful role with the Pats.
WR Mack Hollins: The Patriots love his willingness as a run blocker, but he hadn’t popped much in the passing game until Monday, when he caught three touchdowns in red zone drills and looked like a potential No. 4 option.
WR DeMario Douglas: In Josh McDaniels’ first year back in charge of the offense last season, everyone expected a breakout for Douglas that never arrived. While a massive breakout would be a stretch, he does look more comfortable this camp and could be headed for more targets this season.
WR Efton Chism: The roster crunch gets interesting at receiver, especially if Chism isn’t going to play a big role on special teams. If he doesn’t win the kick-returner gig, it could hurt his 53-man chances.
WR Kyle Williams: After a slow start, Williams appeared to suffer an injury on Saturday and missed Monday’s practice. There’s plenty of time to turn things around, but it’s not how you’d hope his first week of camp would go.
WR Kyle Dixon: He looks the part as a speedy guy who is 6-foot-2 and has a 40-inch vertical leap. But in a crowded receiver room, he’ll need to shine on special teams to earn a surprise spot on the roster.
WR Cameron Dorner: There’s a long way to go for him to make the roster, but Dorner keeps making plays with the third-team unit and could surprise fans (and other teams) by playing well in the preseason.
WR Nick DeGennaro: The target of the deepest pass at Monday’s practice (it was unclear whether DeGennaro or Karon Prunty came down with it), DeGennaro has some big-play ability.
WR Kobe Prentice: Another of the team’s undrafted rookie receivers, Prentice is undersized but has plenty of speed.
TE Hunter Henry: What’s left to be said? He’s steady and always seems to be doing the right things as he enters Year 11 in the NFL.
TE Eli Raridon: The Pats could have been in big trouble after Julian Hill’s season-ending injury if not for a pair of rookies meeting the moment. Raridon needs to get bigger but has impressed with his hands and route running and could be a factor in the passing game this season.
TE Tanner Arkin: The undrafted rookie is big (only one drafted tight end is bigger than Arkin’s 262 pounds) and has shown his strength in run blocking. He may be limited as a route runner, but Arkin can move bodies in the trenches and be a nice complement to Raridon’s skills in the passing game.
TE Jack Westover: He was a jack of all trades a year ago, but it looks like he may be on the wrong side of the roster bubble entering the preseason games.
TE CJ Dippre: An injury has limited the second-year player, but he’s doing some drills to the side during practice, a sign that he could return soon.
TE Mitch Van Vooren: He was a late addition to the training camp roster as the Pats looked to add bodies at tight end. He has a unique background as a former Division I 400-meter hurdler.
TE Jeremiah Franklin: Another late addition, Franklin has probably slim roster chances, but the former Boston College player should get some important reps in the coming weeks as he tries to make the practice squad.
LT Will Campbell: He put a tough postseason behind him and has been really good in training camp. It’ll matter most when games arrive, but it’s a positive sign so far.
LG Alijah Vera-Tucker: The Pats have managed his reps in an attempt to keep him healthy. When he has been on the field, he has absolutely dominated.
C Jared Wilson: There has been plenty of focus on Wilson’s snapping ability before practice as he slides from guard to center.
RG Mike Onwenu: His size stands out among the team’s guards, but he has used it effectively on downhill rushes, and he should still be one of the better players at his position in the NFL.
RT Morgan Moses: Coach Mike Vrabel continues to crack jokes to the team about Moses’ age, but the coach gives him plenty of rest in camp to keep him healthy for the season.
OT Caleb Lomu: It’s been mostly what you’d expect so far from a rookie offensive tackle: a bit up and down, pass protection better than run blocking. He figures to get a few snaps each game (even when Moses is healthy) as a jumbo tight end.
C Ben Brown: His struggles highlight a potential lack of depth for the Patriots on the interior of the O-line.
OT Dametrious Crownover: He’s a fascinating prospect given his size and arm length, but it’ll be important to see how he uses those traits in actual games starting next week.
OT James Hudson III: He moved to guard for some reps on Monday, and his position versatility could be a reason he makes the team.

title: Believing in Drew Brees turned the unbelievable into reality for Saints Larry Holder 6
summary:

full_text:
While a right shoulder injury created doubts about his career, Drew Brees, left, reinvigorated his career with Sean Payton in New Orleans. Chris Graythen / Getty Images
The Athletic has live coverage of NFL training camp .
Sean Payton and Mickey Loomis put on a brave face, knowing they had to publicly sell the idea that Drew Brees would be the New Orleans Saints’ “saving grace” at quarterback, despite being three months removed from his right throwing shoulder basically being shredded during the final week of the 2005 season.
That’s a belief the San Diego Chargers didn’t have in Brees starting in 2004, when they traded for No. 4 overall pick Philip Rivers, and especially after Brees’ shoulder injury.
That’s a belief the Miami Dolphins — at least their medical staff — didn’t share, either. And that’s why Brees ended up in a Hurricane Katrina-ravaged New Orleans rather than Miami.
Predictably, Brees faced immediate questions about that shoulder at his introductory news conference for the Saints. The date was March 14, 2006, and Brees said he would start throwing in mid-to-late April with a rehab program lasting a few months and that he’d be ready by training camp. An almost-defiant Brees answered these two questions:
Do you think you’ll be ready to participate in some preseason games?
Do you have any concern about being able to throw at 100 percent and getting your timing down with your receivers?
If it sounded like Brees was holding a grudge at the time, you couldn’t blame him. While the eventual Hall of Fame quarterback said during training camp in 2010 that wasn’t the case, he questioned whether he got the raw end of the deal.
“You can probably say that in some instances,” Brees said. “But I’ve also learned from this game that, man, this is a business. There’s decisions that are made. Sometimes there’s guys that like you and believe in you. Sometimes they are not, for whatever reason. Sometimes things just seem to be out of your control. You do your best and you hope things work out. But sometimes, your calling is to go somewhere else.
“Life takes you in a different direction.”
That direction took Brees from a discarded quarterback to the Hall of Fame, a journey that also reinvigorated an entire region with a win in Super Bowl XLIV along the way.
It’s the kind of turnaround that takes faith — belief, if you will. The kind of belief few had at the time. The kind of belief that became infectious among Brees’ teammates almost immediately.
“In 2006, we all started looking at each other and started knowing that we weren’t going anywhere without Drew,” former Saints linebacker and Brees teammate Scott Shanle said. “He started making throws and started managing games, and everyone in the locker room could see he was something special.”
Saints general manager Mickey Loomis said at Brees’ first media gathering that Payton brought Brees’ name up from Day 1. “And frankly, I think I heard Drew’s name every single day thereafter …,” Loomis added. No one ever needed to convince Payton, who believes nothing happened by accident when it came to Brees.
“When I was hired by the Saints as head coach in 2006, the very first goal was to establish a functional and winning culture,” Payton said when Brees announced his retirement in March 2021. “In doing so, it was vital to know what we were looking for in a player — talent, work ethic, makeup, intelligence and leadership are all qualities we found in Drew Brees. We also found a player with a burning desire to win. …
“Throughout his career, his consistency and dedication to excellence were unparalleled. In a very short period of time, he would help lead a region to recovery and a team to a Super Bowl championship. He was a magnificent leader both on and off the field. His attention to detail and competitive spirit were infectious. For all of us that have had the chance to coach him, it has been our privilege. We are better for it.”
Former Saints linebacker and Brees teammate Jonathan Vilma joined New Orleans in 2008, when Brees was already well on his way to building a Hall of Fame career. He recalled Brees being “really good, but not great” when the quarterback played for the Chargers. It hit Vilma almost immediately when arriving in New Orleans that something was different with Brees.
“What changed him is when he almost had football taken away from him with the shoulder injury,” Vilma said. “I think that changed him as a competitor and as a person.”
Brees led the Saints to their first NFC Championship Game in his debut season in New Orleans in 2006 and finished runner-up to former Chargers teammate LaDainian Tomlinson as NFL MVP. By the end of 2008, Brees would produce just the NFL’s second 5,000-yard passing season (Dan Marino had the first — 24 years earlier).
Still, what made the NFL landscape truly believe in Brees, and open the door to a Hall of Fame career, occurred during the 2009 season.
The Brees-led Saints won 16 games combined in the regular season and playoffs, including a 13-0 start that year. He tacked on another NFL MVP runner-up accolade, losing to New Orleans native Peyton Manning. But he became his own piece of Crescent City NFL royalty by earning the MVP of Super Bowl XLIV as the Saints toppled Manning and the Indianapolis Colts.
Along the way, Brees stared NFL QB nobility in the face and took each player down one by one.
Since at least 2000, he’s the only Super Bowl-winning quarterback to play heads up against three Hall of Fame quarterbacks (Manning, Brett Favre, Kurt Warner) and either Tom Brady or Aaron Rodgers (certain future Hall of Famers) in one season and finish with a 4-0 record. In those four games, he threw 13 touchdown passes and no interceptions with a 72 percent completion rate, leading to a 133.5 passer rating and a 0.50 EPA, via TruMedia.
Despite entering a Week 12 unbeaten that season, Brees and the Saints still believed they were not in the same category as Brady and the Patriots, their opponents that week for a Monday Night Football clash.
“I definitely think if you just stood the two of us next to each other, we wouldn’t look anything alike, so maybe you’d say that our styles are a little different,” Brees said leading up to the game. “But in the end, you want the result to be the same: You win football games and you win championships. Obviously, (Brady) has three, and I’m still trying to get that first.”
In front of a national television audience, Brees produced a perfect 158.3 passer rating, throwing for 317 yards and five touchdowns as the Saints trounced the Patriots 38-17. Bill Belichick pulled Brady from the game midway through the fourth quarter, raising a white flag.
“It only counts for one win on the stat sheet, but emotionally, those types of wins can mean a little more,” Brees said after the game.
Wildly enough, this would be the fourth time Brady hit the bench during a game against Brees in their collegiate and professional careers.
The Saints limped into the playoffs after losing their final three regular-season games. And there may have been some non-belief in Brees from the Arizona side. Cardinals safety Antrel Rolle said leading up to this game that he’d rather face Brees any day of the week rather than Rodgers, despite getting past the Packers in the NFC Wild Card round.
“We got out with that mentality that, hey, every time we touch the ball we want to go out and score,” Brees said during game week.
And that just about happened. Brees alone didn’t easily dispose of the Cardinals, thanks to one of Reggie Bush’s most memorable NFL performances and a swarming Saints defense. But Brees threw for three touchdowns and 247 yards, resulting in a 125.4 passer rating to ease the Saints to the NFC title game.

full_text:
Renardo Green is off to a strong start in his third season after being challenged by the 49ers' coaching staff. Sergio Estrada / Imagn Images
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — Renardo Green heard the trade rumors this offseason. Then he saw the San Francisco 49ers sign a cornerback who could push him for his starting job.
Then Green made an interesting move: He watched the newcomer, veteran Jack Jones, during offseason workouts and the first week of training camp and actually learned some things from him.
“Jack and I have had a lot of conversations,” Green said. “He’s a real savvy football player, and Jack has real good ball skills. He has a very aggressive playing style when it comes to playing the ball, and I try and pick that up.
“You should try to learn from who you can because we’re all in this together, basically.”
Jones, 28, is on his fourth team in five years, but no one questions his playmaking ability — good and bad. He started 33 games for the Las Vegas Raiders and Miami Dolphins over the past two seasons and had 22 pass breakups. He has returned half of his eight career interceptions for touchdowns.
Jones has been a standout at training camp. And one of the only players you could say has stood out more is Green, who dominated one-on-one drills on Monday.
“He’s a great corner,” Jones said of Green. “I think he has the potential to be one of the true lockdown corners in the league, you know what I’m saying? As far as from me to him, I’ve just been trying to really tell him to go get that ball. Focus on the ball and not just PBUs.
“That’s what I am preaching. … We’re all making each other better. A guy makes a play, and that gives you an energy boost.”
Raheem Morris has been a big part of that, and Green is really enjoying his third defensive coordinator in three years. You get the sense that the 2024 second-round pick is not just saying that because it’s what people want to hear.
“It’s easier to play faster, and I feel like he’s more detailed with just, like, realistic things, and there’s a lot less thinking,” Green said. “I’ve been able to get attached to guys and contest catches, make plays. That’s what he wants, and that fits us.”
When general manager John Lynch was asked about the offseason trade rumors involving Green, he pointed at Morris.
“Raheem is really excited to work with Renardo,” Lynch said. “He sees tools that are untapped. He can be a big-time player. He hasn’t been bad by any account, but we think there’s a lot more in there.”
That was the message from coach Kyle Shanahan. The trade rumors surrounding Green stemmed from a sideline exchange during the playoff loss to the Seahawks, where Shanahan was yelling at Green for a blown coverage. Shanahan said that was a good sign — that he expects a lot from Green — and that he wouldn’t yell if he didn’t think a player had a higher ceiling.
Green said he appreciated it.
“He and I talk, and how he sees me is similar to how I see myself and what I’m capable of doing, everything I want out of this game,” Green said. “So I appreciate him for just pushing me. It gives you more confidence just to work harder, because you know that you’re not going to let yourself slack but you know he’s not going to let you slack, either.”
Morris has been impressed.
“He’s showing up in a big way,” Morris said. “He’s exciting. He’s got great length. He’s got great ball skills. He’s got all the ability in the world. It’s time to go out there and do it.”
Right now, Green is slated to line up across from Deommodore Lenoir, with Upton Stout in the slot. Lenoir said he and Green spent a lot of time together this offseason, and Green is a new man. He’s talking more and “is more confident in his craft,” Lenoir said.
“Just being able to come in, Year 3, and have the confidence to backpedal against a Hall of Fame receiver (Mike Evans) and being poised,” Lenoir added. “I think he’s taking a big step in that direction.”
As for Jones, before he signed, he heard rave reviews about the 49ers from good friend Chase Lucas, who spent two years with the Niners before signing with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in April.
“I love it,” Jones said. “Great energy, great, great teammates. … It’s kind of self-explanatory why this team has had the success that it has. Shoutout to Chase Lucas.”
Jones is here to compete, obviously, but he could give the 49ers some great depth while helping bring out the best in Green, Lenoir and Stout. Lenoir has eight interceptions in five seasons, but Green and Stout have one between them.
“People don’t just wake up with that ability to go get the ball,” Jones said. “It comes with film study, it comes with practice and repetition. Sometimes you got to take a million reps just to get it right one time.
“I played receiver too growing up. But I didn’t want to get thrown the ball. I wanted to go take it.”

title: Stefon Diggs to the Commanders would be another NFL homecoming. Is that a positive? As Stefon Diggs remains a free agent and Washington needs a wideout, it's worth remembering that playing at home isn't always a benefit. Barry Svrluga 6

The Athletic has live coverage of NFL training camp .
ASHBURN, Va. — Nick Cross was born in Bowie, Md. He played high school football at DeMatha Catholic High School in nearby Hyattsville. His college ball came at the University of Maryland, just around the corner.
So when Cross became a free agent this spring, and the Washington
full_text:
Tim Settle, who grew up in Northern Virginia, was drafted by Washington's NFL franchise and then returned to D.C. in the 2026 offseason. Mitchell Layton / Getty Images
The Athletic has live coverage of NFL training camp .
ASHBURN, Va. — Nick Cross was born in Bowie, Md. He played high school football at DeMatha Catholic High School in nearby Hyattsville. His college ball came at the University of Maryland, just around the corner.
So when Cross became a free agent this spring, and the Washington Commanders had an opening at safety and a contract offer for Cross, it was a no-brainer, right?
Play your home games in the same county where you were born, raised and played your high school and college careers? Anyone would sign up, it would seem.
“You want to go where you can play and put your skills on display,” Cross said. “You want to go where you’re going to have an opportunity, and where you think you can win. That’s all that matters for me in football — put my skills on display, and go out there and do my thing.”
Which brings us to one of the most discussed people at Commanders’ training camp who actually isn’t at Commanders’ training camp. (No, not Brandon Aiyuk. Let’s put him and his high-Instagram rate to the side for a while.)
That would be Stefon Diggs. The veteran receiver grew up in Gaithersburg, Md., a short drive from Washington. He went to Good Counsel High in nearby Olney. He, too, played collegiately at Maryland.
He’s a free agent. The conventional wisdom — outside team headquarters here, at least — is that the Commanders need more talent and depth at wide receiver . Diggs is coming off an 85-catch, 1,013-yard season with New England — his seventh 1,000-yard campaign in the last eight years.
Shouldn’t a homecoming be a layup?
“It’s not always that simple,” said Tim Settle Jr., a Commanders’ defensive tackle now, a lineman growing up at what’s now known as Unity Reed High School in Manassas, Va.
Here’s the thing: The idea of professional athletes playing at home seems ideal. In practice, it can be tough. Home might be where your closest and oldest friends are. But home can be where the hangers-on are, too.
“If they can reach me,” Settle said, smiling. “You got to be smart about it.”
Settle was drafted by Washington out of Virginia Tech in 2018. He left as a free agent for Buffalo in 2022, and returned to Washington this offseason after two more seasons in Houston. He knows what it’s like to build a professional life in surroundings both completely familiar and absolutely foreign.
“I got my fanbases out here,” Settle said. “I’m more recognized here. It’s just a familiarity with the area, and people are familiar with me. I know when I go somewhere, I got higher praise here than I would in, like, Texas.
“I could stay at my grandma’s house tonight if I wanted to. I wouldn’t even have to ask.”
Those are the benefits, and they’re obvious.
“It’s good to be around my mom, my dad,” said Cross, who understands that getting around Beltway traffic from Ashburn to Bowie isn’t like living across the street. “But there are drawbacks to anywhere you play.”
There are some examples of drawbacks in Washington’s recent past. Chase Young played collegiately at Ohio State, but he grew up in Prince George’s County, Md., and played at St. Vincent Pallotti High School before transferring to DeMatha. When Washington made him the second overall pick in the 2020 draft, it seemed a perfect hit — a hometown kid returning to help resurrect the team for which he grew up rooting.
It didn’t work out. That’s in part because then-head coach Ron Rivera and his staff proved overmatched in assembling a roster and coaching it up. But it says here that Young didn’t benefit from playing near home.
Take October of 2023, by which time Young had missed time after blowing out his knee and had underproduced when he was on the field. On the afternoon “Grant and Danny” radio show on 106.7 The Fan, co-host Grant Paulsen used some time to do what radio hosts do: break down numbers and discuss performance. It’s OK to fairly criticize these players. That’s the job. Let’s take some calls.
Well, darned if the station phone didn’t ring, and damned if it wasn’t Greg Young — Chase’s dad — on the other end .
“Do you have the numbers of how much he’s double- and triple-teamed compared to the other guys?” Greg Young challenged Paulsen.
And off they went. Greg Young cited some statistics to try to defend his kid. Paulsen pushed back on those numbers. Entertaining and unexpected stuff.
The point isn’t whether Greg Young was right or wrong. (For clarification, he was wrong.) The point is a grown man being paid millions of dollars to perform professionally doesn’t need his parents driving around in cars listening to radio criticism and then calling the station in their defense. It’s not healthy.
Sure, that’s an extreme example. But it’s cautionary. Home is where the heart is? Fine. It isn’t always the best place to develop professionally.
“There’s a lot to consider when you’re making a choice,” Cross said. “But the fit and the opportunity have to be what’s most important.”
Which brings us back to Diggs. Forget where he grew up. Wouldn’t the fit and opportunity be perfect in Washington? Through the first four workouts of training camp, the Commanders have put some combination of Treylon Burks, Van Jefferson and Luke McCaffrey alongside top wideout Terry McLaurin with the first-team offense. Total catches in 2025 for that group: 50. Or 35 fewer than Diggs had on his own.
The Commanders, a person with knowledge of the situation said, are keeping tabs on Diggs. Diggs, who occasionally worked out at the Maryland facility this summer, appears content to see if he can land a two-year deal even as he turns 33 in November.
So the dance goes on. Cross signed with his hometown team this offseason, but not because it was his hometown team. Somewhere out there, Diggs is hoping he has options. Maybe one will be his hometown team. That could be a plus — or not.
“There’s way more to think about,” Cross said.

title: Arizona Cardinals HC Has Three-Word Answer on Josh Sweat's Week 1 Status
full_text:
GLENDALE — Josh Sweat has yet to make an appearance for the Arizona Cardinals in 2026.
That dates back to offseason team activities, where he wasn't present before he was on the sidelines for mandatory minicamp. At the beginning of training camp, the Cardinals placed him on PUP, and he's yet to come off the list.
He hasn't been spotted on the sidelines during practice, either.
Sweat doesn't appear likely to play in the preseason, and as speculation swirls around what exactly is happening with Arizona's top pass rusher, the Cardinals are confident he'll be ready for the regular season.
"I do. Yes," said head coach Mike LaFleur when asked if he'll be ready for Week 1.
Sweat has been a consistent topic surrounding the Cardinals despite not being on the field after early reports of a trade request this offseason. LaFleur, asked earlier in camp on Sweat , insisted there was no discontent on his end before adding:
"He's always stayed away in those phase one, phase two, phase three [periods]. He was working with our team pretty good. And he was around. That's what Josh has done, and that's what's worked for Josh to get himself in position to play the best football, and we knew that. Not that I was here a year ago, but we knew that when we brought him in. I knew that when I first got here in February.
"So the cool part about Josh is everyone's been on the same page the entire time. You guys can believe me or not, I'm not worried about Josh Sweat at all in terms of his health and all that. [He needs] a little bit more time, he's logged a lot of miles in this league as well. I think not only for Josh to peak on September 13, but Josh to also get through the rigors of a 17-game season the way that he plays and the motor that he plays with, I think this is best for him and the Cardinals."
Sweat's 12 sacks last season were nearly double of the second-highest Cardinals player in Calais Campbell (6.5), who is no longer with the team. The next-highest individual totals were two sacks each from Baron Browning and Walter Nolen III.
Sweat's presence within Arizona's defense is vital for the Cardinals entering the 2026 season, as the team made virtually zero improvements to its pass rush over the course of the offseason.

title: Trey Benson Trade Buzz Growing Louder After Cardinals Roster Moves
full_text:
GLENDALE — Trade buzz continues to heighten around over Arizona Cardinals running back Trey Benson.
Benson was not spotted at yesterday's practice — not even dressed on the sideline — and head coach Mike LaFleur (who is pretty good at keeping reporters updated via injury) didn't mention his potential absence ahead of Sunday's practice.
There was already trade speculation around Benson entering his third season in the league, though his absence yesterday was followed today by the Cardinals claiming running back Evan Hull while working out fellow ball-carrier Jermar Jefferson, which only ignited that speculation.
The #AZCardinals waived DL Coziah Izzard and WR Tejhaun Palmer and claimed DT Cam Horsley and RB Evan Hull. Cardinals also tried out RB Jermar Jefferson. Notable since RB Trey Benson was not spotted at practice yesterday
LaFleur says his absence was due to injury:
"Just a little discomfort, little flare up in the left knee. It's unfortunate because he was feeling so good, and I thought he was really getting his legs underneath him. I thought he strung together some good days. It was good news today that he was feeling much better," he told reporters ahead of Monday.
Benson has been an obvious trade candidate for the Cardinals since the arrival of Tyler Allgeier (free agency) and Jeremiyah Love (draft) — on top of James Conner, who restructured his contract to stay with the team for 2026.
A former Day 2 draft pick, Benson's early career in Arizona has been marked by injuries and inconsistent opportunity/play. He's shown the ability to pop off a big run, similar to his days at Florida State, though he's yet to realize his full potential in the Cardinals' backfield.
The Cardinals seem intent on running the ball plenty, though with such a top heavy backfield in Allgeier/Love/Conner, Benson is very much on the outside looking in.
He was named a loser in our winners/losers of training camp so far, which you can find here .
Not only has Benson's role in Arizona's offense taken a hit — his chances of being on the roster have as well. Benson was listed as RB4 on the Cardinals' first depth chart, though Bam Knight has seen more team work ahead of Benson as we enter Arizona's first preseason game.
Knight very well could get a final nod thanks to special teams work if a decision comes down between the two of them. Benson has seen limited action during 11 v 11 opportunities, and when he has participated, it's been with the third team.
The Cardinals, in an ideal world, would trade Benson before cutting him for a late-round pick. There's plenty of running back-needy teams who would send a flyer to get Benson, who simply might need a change of scenery to thrive.
Benson has played 17 games for the Cardinals across his two NFL seasons. He ended on injured reserve both seasons with an ankle (2024) and knee (2025) injuries. On 92 rushes he's averaged 4.9 yards per carry with one touchdown to his name.

title: Jacoby Brissett's Actual Cardinals Contract Includes Surprising Salary Cap Decision
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals finally have Jacoby Brissett's contract dilemma behind them.
Arizona reached a reworked deal with their starting quarterback to give Brissett a pay raise ahead of 2026. Initial reports indicated he had a contract of $15.5 million that could be worth up to $21 million with incentives with no additional years added, still making him a free agent after this season.
The actual numbers have emerged from Brissett's deal, and the bookkeeping on Arizona's part to get over the finish line was interesting.
Base Salary : $9.7 million Prorated Signing Bonus : $8.97 million Workout Bonus : $50,000 Other Bonus : $240,000 Guaranteed Salary : $9.7 million 2026 Cap Number : $10.365 million
In total, Brissett got roughly $10 million guaranteed in raises.
Brissett's cap figure for 2026 only jumped by $1.175 million after the new deal.
Brissett had a void year added to his contract, which will carry a $7.22 million hit next season. It was interesting to note the Cardinals opted to not absorb the entire pay raise this offseason.
That was a similar route they took when cutting Kyler Murray, choosing to split his dead cap hit into two offseasons as opposed to just 2026. Brissett will join Murray in 2027 dead cap space if he doesn't play in Arizona, who also carries a $7.2 million dead cap hit next offseason similar to Brissett.
As CardsWire's Howard Balzer notes , the extra incentive money to get the contract up to $21 million as first pushed is also not listed on the actual figures of the contract.
"The only incentive listed is $45,000 for a likely to be earned incentive that isn’t known and counts against the cap immediately and $240,000 in unlikely to be earned incentives that don’t count, but would in 2027 if they are reached. That $45,000 is included in the $10.365 million mentioned earlier," he said.
The Cardinals were able to give Brissett the rise in pay he wanted ahead of 2026 without breaking the bank, though Arizona's willingness to take future charges on Brissett and Murray (which will total over $14 million next offseason assuming Brissett doesn't play for the Cardinals) is odd given the current state of the team and ample cap space available for Arizona this season.
The Cardinals currently rank eighth in the NFL in terms of cap space at $33.8 million.

title: Everything We've Learned About Cardinals' Backup QB Battle So Far
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals ' quarterback situation has dominated headlines since the early days of the offseason.
That's not going to slow down anytime soon.
Jacoby Brissett signed his reworked contract and is fully set to be the team's starter ahead of 2026. For how long, nobody knows. The Cardinals, if bad as projected, will likely make a change under center at some point.
For that reason, Arizona's backup quarterback situation is still very much worth investing in for both preseason and regular season purposes.
What we've learned about the backup battle so far:
Slovis, who was in Arizona last season as their practice squad guy, never really had a chance to crack the active roster this year after Gardner Minshew and Carson Beck entered the picture.
Slovis practically would have needed to make a massive jump and played the best football of his life to really make the Cardinals think twice on cutting him. Unfortunately, that hasn't happened, and his football future really seems like it will be shaping up outside of Arizona after the preseason barring injury.
When you think of a prototypical gun-slinger at quarterback, Minshew fits that mold. He's been letting it rip in training camp, pushing the ball all across the field and taking chances. That's led to some exciting plays, though that's also led to some turnovers in the process.
Minshew's overall body of work in camp mixed with his veteran experience has placed him firmly in the QB2 spot. If Arizona were to need an alternate option besides Brissett, Minshew is undoubtedly their guy.
At this moment in time, Minshew would be the immediate replacement in the Cardinals make a swap in the regular season. However, thanks to numerous factors, Beck looms behind him — and Minshew would have to play exceptionally high to prevent the rookie from playing at all in 2026.
I dove exceptionally deeper on this topic (which you can read here ), but the Cardinals have a massive quarterback decision looming after this season, which Beck will have an unknown amount of say in. Case in point, Arizona needs to see their most recent investment on the field as much as possible to form an opinion (one way or another).
Beck has been a second fiddle to Minshew during camp, and rightfully so. Besides Minshew getting the nod thanks to experience, Beck's overall play in training camp practices has been across the board. His start was forgettable thanks to accuracy issues, though in the last few days he's really turned a corner .
That can make for some good overreactions , but the reality is Beck is still the wildcard out of this group. At some point it feels like he'll play, though we are far removed from this.
However, all dominoes eventually lead to Beck later in the regular season.
